common.neutral: After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder.
common.preSay: Two sneak-peek puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, so is I do not know. Nobody is marked. Say your answer together on three.
preDo: Show the Sneak-peek puzzles slide at minute 1.5 (4.5 minutes: about 45 seconds for question 1, 90 seconds for question 2, then the answers). Say the short line out loud (about 28 words): two puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet; guessing and "I do not know" are welcome; nobody is marked; say your answer together on three. Read each puzzle aloud; question 1 is the one to start with (objects, a drawing or counting).

Answers stay private. Each child writes the answer on their own paper, ticks it against the answer slide, and says it together on three (nothing is held up to the camera; do not read answers out). Never raise whiteboards together and never show a board in front of the group. Never ask a named child "how do you know?" Ask for volunteers: "Would anyone like to tell us how they started?"

Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Question 2 is the thinking question. Do not mark either one. Click to show the answers at the end as "one way to think about it", without saying who had what.

Use what you see only to plan. Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group. Children choose, and may move either way at any time. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Everybody joins the explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.
common.talkDo: You choose volunteers first: "Who would like to share?" If nobody offers, ask the pairs to share what their partner said. Never cold-call a child by name. Any child may say "pass" at any time and that is always fine. Do not keep public tallies, scores or rankings (no counting who got most right, no "first to finish"). Invite the whole group to think about whether they would like a turn, never one child.
common.refSay: Looking back takes 2 minutes. Find the box called Looking back on the page “Before you go: Investigation and Looking back”. Finish one line, two lines or all three, and tick what helped you. You may pass on any line. If you tick "I am still stuck", your tutor will check in during the session.
common.refDo: Nothing is collected in front of the group and nobody has to read theirs out. The tutor may read a box while stamping journals (never by private message), and checks in on a child who ticked still stuck during the open session, for example by a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal with a parent nearby, for example "I saw you drew it when you got stuck". A child may volunteer one sentence, never by name unless they choose to. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the next open session (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby). Praise the strategy, not the speed.
common.close: Closing and stamps take the last minute and a half (88.5 to 90).

pre.q: Mei has 3 hundreds, 2 tens and 5 ones. Draw them if you like. What number is that?
pre.w: Hundreds first, then tens, then ones. A drawing of 3 flats, 2 rods and 5 units is welcome. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: Mei has digit cards 4, 0 and 7. She uses each card once to make a 3-digit number. How many different numbers can she make? Write them.
pre.w: 0 cannot be the hundreds digit, so only 4 and 7 can start. Listing in order: 4 starts 2 numbers, 7 starts 2 numbers. A child who says 6 is using 3 x 2 x 1 without the zero rule: a good idea, not a mistake to correct yet.

invest.title: Mirror numbers
invest.first: Easy first step: write 252, 909 and 131, then write three more mirror numbers.
invest.text: A mirror number reads the same forwards and backwards, like 252 or 909. (a) Write 5 mirror numbers of your own. (b) Find ALL the mirror numbers from 200 to 299. How do you know you have found them all? (c) Ali says every mirror number is odd. Is he right?
invest.model: (a) Any number whose first and last digits match, such as 101, 454, 777. (b) 10 numbers: 202, 212, 222, 232, 242, 252, 262, 272, 282, 292. The first and last digits must both be 2, and the middle digit can be 0 to 9: 10 choices. A child who lists them by the middle digit in order has not missed any. (c) No: 202 is even. A mirror number is even when its first (and last) digit is even. Extension: there are 90 mirror numbers from 100 to 999 (9 choices for the end digits x 10 for the middle). Look for: the child sees that the end digits match, lists in order, and can say why the list is complete.

whatif.q: Go further: add a fourth card, 2. Use any THREE of the cards 2, 3, 5 and 8. How many different 3-digit numbers can you make?
whatif.a: 24: 4 choices of which card to leave out, and each set of 3 cards makes 6 numbers (4 x 6 = 24).

pre.q: 3{box}2 + 416 = 788. Which digit is hidden in the box? (Use counters or draw the columns if it helps.)
pre.w: No carry in this one: look at the tens column, 1 and what makes 8. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: 4{box}6 + 237 = 683. Which digit is hidden in the box? How do you know?
pre.w: Ones: 6 + 7 = 13, so 1 ten is carried. Tens: the box + 3 + 1 must end in 8, so the box is 4. Listen for: "carry", or a guess that was tested and checked.

invest.title: Odd or even?
invest.first: Easy first step: use counters to try 3 + 5, 7 + 9 and 11 + 13. Are the answers odd or even?
invest.text: Ali says: "When I add two odd numbers, I always get an even number." (a) Test Ali's idea with 5 pairs of odd 3-digit numbers (for example 345 + 271). (b) Now test odd + even, and even + even. What do you notice? (c) Explain WHY, using pairs of counters or a drawing.
invest.model: (a) Ali is right: odd + odd is always even (checked for every pair of 3-digit numbers). (b) Odd + even is always odd; even + even is always even. (c) Why: an odd number is some pairs plus 1 left over, an even number is only pairs. Two odd numbers have two left-overs, and they make one more pair, so no one is left over. Look for: several tests before a claim, then a reason that uses pairs, counters or ones digits, not only "it worked every time". A ones-digit reason (odd ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9) is also fine. Extension (not printed): taking away behaves the same way: odd − odd is even, odd − even is odd.

whatif.q: Go further: now make 1000. What is the partner of 358 that makes 1000 (358 + ? = 1000)? What do you notice about the columns?
whatif.a: 642. Ones: 8 + 2 = 10. Tens: 5 + 4 + 1 = 10. Hundreds: 3 + 6 + 1 = 10. Every column carries.

unstuck: tried a digit and checked it

pre.q: A tray has 3 rows of counters with 5 counters in each row. Draw it if you like. How many counters are there?
pre.w: Counting in 5s, or drawing and counting. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: A toy shop has cars (4 wheels) and scooters (2 wheels). 6 toys have 16 wheels altogether. How many cars and how many scooters? How do you know?
pre.w: Starting with all scooters (12 wheels) and swapping one at a time is the idea of today. A child who draws 6 vehicles and counts wheels is thinking well. Guess and check is welcome.

invest.title: Where tables meet
invest.first: Easy first step: write the 5 times table up to 50, then circle the even numbers.
invest.text: (a) List the numbers up to 50 that are in BOTH the 2 times table and the 5 times table. What do you notice about them? (b) Now find the numbers up to 50 that are in both the 3 and 5 tables. (c) Is every number in both the 2 and 5 tables also in the 10 table? Explain.
invest.model: (a) 10, 20, 30, 40, 50: they jump by 10 and are the 10 times table. (b) 3 and 5: 15, 30, 45 (jump by 15). (Extension: 4 and 5 give 20, 40, jump by 20.) (c) Yes to both, brute-forced up to 100: a number in the 10 table is 10 x something = 2 x (5 x something) = 5 x (2 x something). Child-level reason: a number in the 2 table is even and a number in the 5 table ends in 0 or 5, so a number in both ends in 0, which is the 10 table; and every number in the 10 table ends in 0, so it is even and in the 5 table. Look for: organised lists (writing both tables out and circling), the noticing that the jumps are 10, 15, 20, and a test of “always”.

whatif.q: Go further: what if the farmer counts 20 legs? How many different mixes of hens and goats are there now?
whatif.a: 6 mixes: 10 hens; 8 hens and 1 goat; 6 hens and 2 goats; 4 hens and 3 goats; 2 hens and 4 goats; 5 goats.

pre.q: Draw this pattern up to the 9th shape: circle, circle, square, circle, circle, square ... What is the 9th shape?
pre.a: A square (the squares are the 3rd, 6th and 9th shapes).
pre.w: Drawing it out is a fine method. Listen for "every 3rd one is a square".

pre.q: A pattern repeats: star, moon, moon, sun, star, moon, moon, sun ... What is the 22nd shape? How do you know?
pre.w: Groups of 4: 20 is the end of a group (5 groups of 4), so the 21st is a star and the 22nd is a moon. Drawing 22 shapes is also fine.

invest.title: Three counting patterns
invest.first: Easy first step: write pattern A, 1, 4, 7, 10 ..., up to 30.
invest.text: Pattern A: 1, 4, 7, 10 ... (add 3 each time). Pattern B: 2, 5, 8, 11 ... Pattern C: 3, 6, 9, 12 ... (a) Write each pattern up to 30. (b) Pick any number from 1 to 30. Which pattern is it in? Can a number be in two patterns? Can a number be in none? (c) Why does this happen?
invest.model: (a) A: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28. B: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 29. C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. (b) Every number is in exactly ONE pattern (brute-forced for 1 to 99). (c) Counting in 3s, a number is either on the 3s (pattern C), 1 more than a number on the 3s (A), or 2 more (B); there is no other choice. Extension (not printed): if each pattern added 4 you would need 4 patterns, starting at 1, 2, 3 and 4. Look for: a complete listing, the claim “exactly one” tested on more than one number, and a reason that uses the 3 times table.

whatif.q: Go further: what if the cube train is red, red, blue, green, red, red, blue, green ...? What colour is cube 20? What colour is cube 30?
whatif.a: Cube 20 is green (the green cubes are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20). Cube 30 is red (28 is green, 29 and 30 are red).

pre.q: A machine adds 7. The OUT is 12. What was the IN? (Count back with counters if you like.)
pre.w: IN is what goes in and OUT is what comes out. Undo = do the opposite: 12 - 7. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: A machine doubles, then adds 7. The OUT is 17. What was the IN? How do you know?
pre.w: Undo the last step first: 17 - 7 = 10, then half of 10 is 5. A guess that was tested (5 x 2 + 7 = 17) is just as good.

invest.title: A magic trick
invest.first: Easy first step: do the trick with 3, then with 10, and write down each step.
invest.text: Think of a number. Add 5. Double it. Take away 10. Halve it. (a) Try 5 different starting numbers. What do you notice about your final answer? (b) Is it ALWAYS true? Try a big number and a small number, then say why. (c) Make your own trick that always gives you back the number you started with. Test it on 3 numbers.
invest.model: (a) The final answer is always the number you started with (brute-forced for 1 to 999). (b) Adding 5 then doubling adds 10 and doubles the start; taking away 10 and halving undoes both: (n + 5) x 2 − 10 = n x 2, and half of that is n. A child reason: “double and halve undo each other, and add 5 doubled is 10, which I take away”. (c) Any valid trick, for example: add 3, double, take away 6, halve; or times 4, add 8, divide by 4, take away 2. Check by testing three numbers. Look for: testing small and big numbers, a reason in words, and a trick that really works.

whatif.q: Go further: what if the machine adds 7 FIRST and then doubles? Put IN 5 into it. Is the OUT the same as before (17)?
whatif.a: No: 5 + 7 = 12, doubled is 24. The order of the steps matters.

pre.q: Mei has one 50¢ coin, one 20¢ coin and one 10¢ coin. How much money is that? Use play coins or draw them.
pre.w: Counting on from the biggest coin. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: Mei has $5. Three drinks cost $1.60 each. Does she have enough? How much money is left?
pre.a: Yes. 3 drinks cost $4.80, so 20¢ is left.
pre.w: Listen for adding $1.60 three times, or $1 + $1 + $1 and then 60¢ three times (180¢ = $1.80). Counting up from $4.80 to $5 is a good method.

invest.title: Most coins
invest.need: Needs: play coins (5¢, 10¢, 20¢, 50¢), or paper and a pencil.
invest.first: Easy first step: pay 35¢ with the fewest coins from the 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ coins.
invest.text: Use only 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ coins. (a) Pay 35¢ using the fewest coins. How many coins is that? (b) Try the other amounts from 5¢ to 95¢ (in steps of 5¢) and make a table of how many coins each needs. (c) Which amount needs the MOST coins, even when you use the fewest possible?
invest.model: Fewest coins (5¢ to 95¢): 5:1, 10:1, 15:2, 20:1, 25:2, 30:2, 35:3, 40:2, 45:3, 50:1, 55:2, 60:2, 65:3, 70:2, 75:3, 80:3, 85:4, 90:3, 95:4 (brute-forced). (a) 35¢ = 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢, 3 coins. (c) 85¢ and 95¢ need 4 coins each: 85¢ = 50¢ + 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ and 95¢ = 50¢ + 20¢ + 20¢ + 5¢. An amount ending in 5 needs a 5¢ coin, and the rest then needs 3 more coins. Look for: a systematic table, trying biggest coin first, and checking that no smaller number of coins works.

whatif.q: Go further: what if the toy stall also sells a robot for $5? Now how many different baskets cost exactly $10? (At most one of each toy.)
whatif.a: 5 baskets: kite + ball; kite + yo-yo + sticker; ball + sticker + robot; yo-yo + bubbles + robot; ball + yo-yo + bubbles + sticker.

pre.q: Fold a paper strip (or draw a bar) into 2 equal parts. Colour 1 part. What fraction is coloured?
pre.w: Equal parts matter. Folding on camera is welcome. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: Ali has 1/5 of a roti prata. Mei has 1/8 of the same prata. Who has more? How do you know?
pre.a: Ali (1/5). The same prata cut into fewer parts gives bigger parts.
pre.w: Many children say 1/8 because 8 is bigger. Draw two strips, one cut in 5 and one cut in 8, and compare. A drawing is a good answer.

invest.title: Fraction strips
invest.need: Needs: the fraction strips from the cut-out page (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, eighths).
invest.first: Easy first step: lay the two quarter strips on top of the half strip. Do they fit exactly?
invest.text: (a) Cover a HALF strip exactly with pieces of ONE kind only. Which kinds work? How many pieces of each? (b) Do the same for a THIRD strip and a QUARTER strip. (c) Can thirds ever cover a half exactly? Why not?
invest.model: (a) Half: 2 quarters, 3 sixths or 4 eighths (not thirds). (b) Third: 2 sixths only. Quarter: 2 eighths only (checked with exact fractions). (c) No: one third is shorter than a half but two thirds is longer, so no number of thirds fits exactly. Look for: children lay the strips side by side and say “fits exactly”. Keep to the strips and drawings: do not teach “equivalent fractions” as a rule (that is P3).

whatif.q: Go further: fold a strip into 3 equal parts. How do you know the parts are equal? Then fold one into 6 equal parts: how many sixths make a half? A third?
whatif.a: Thirds: fold and adjust until the 3 parts match, then check one part on top of another. 3 sixths make a half and 2 sixths make a third.

pre.q: A stack has 2 layers. Each layer has 2 rows of 3 cubes. How many cubes are in the stack? (Build it with cubes or draw it.)
pre.w: Counting one layer first, then doubling, is a good method. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: A shape is made of 2 half circles and 1 quarter circle. If you cut every piece into quarter circles, how many quarter circles do you get?
pre.w: Listen for "a half circle is half of a circle, which is 2 quarters". Drawing the pieces and cutting them is fine.

invest.title: Squares joined edge to edge
invest.need: Needs: square tiles or small squares of paper, and the grid on this page.
invest.first: Easy first step: join 2 squares edge to edge. How many different shapes can you make? Then add a third square.
invest.text: Squares must touch along a whole side. A shape that is turned round or flipped over counts as the SAME shape. (a) Find ALL the different shapes you can make with 3 squares. (b) Now find ALL the different shapes you can make with 4 squares. Draw each one on the grid. (c) How do you know you have found them all?
invest.model: (a) 2 shapes: a straight line and an L. (b) 5 shapes: a straight line of 4, a 2 x 2 square, an L, a T and a zigzag (S shape). Brute-forced: 1, 1, 2, 5 shapes for 1, 2, 3, 4 squares (turns and flips count as the same). If a child counts flips as different, they find 7 (L and its mirror, S and its mirror): praise this and explain the rule. (c) Look for a system: start with the straight line, then move one square, and check each new shape against the others by turning the tile.

whatif.q: Go further: you have 2 half circles and 3 quarter circles. How many whole circles can you make? What is left over?
whatif.a: 7 quarter circles in all: 1 whole circle (4 quarters) and 3 quarters left over.

pre.q: You have a 3 ℓ jug and a 5 ℓ jug. You fill the 5 ℓ jug and pour from it into the 3 ℓ jug until the 3 ℓ jug is full. How much water is left in the 5 ℓ jug? (Try it with two cups and rice, or draw it.)
pre.w: One pour is enough. This is a first win for everyone and previews the pour table.

pre.q: A melon balances 2 apples. One apple balances 3 plums. How many plums balance the melon? How do you know?
pre.w: Listen for swapping: the melon can be swapped for 2 apples, and each apple for 3 plums. Drawing the scale is a good method.

invest.title: Weights puzzle
invest.need: Needs: paper and a pencil (cubes or coins can stand for the weights).
invest.first: Easy first step: with weights of 1 g, 2 g and 4 g, can you make 3 g? Can you make 5 g?
invest.text: You have three different weights. Each weight is 1 g, 2 g, 3 g, 4 g or 5 g. You put some of them on one pan to make a mass. (a) With weights of 1 g, 2 g and 4 g, which masses from 1 g to 7 g can you make? (b) Find ALL the sets of three different weights from 1 g to 5 g that can make every mass from 1 g to 6 g. (c) What do all the good sets have in common?
invest.model: (a) All of them: 1, 2, 1+2 = 3, 4, 1+4 = 5, 2+4 = 6, 1+2+4 = 7. (b) Exactly 2 sets work: 1, 2, 3 (makes 1 to 6) and 1, 2, 4 (makes 1 to 7); brute-forced over all 10 sets. (c) Both contain 1 g and 2 g: only a 1 g weight can make 1 g, and with different weights only a 2 g weight can make 2 g. Look for: a systematic list of the possible sets, checking each mass in order, and the noticing that 1 g is needed.

whatif.q: Go further: one glue stick balances 8 coins. A pencil case balances 3 glue sticks. How many coins balance the pencil case? If an eraser balances 4 coins, how many erasers balance the pencil case?

pre.q: A box has 3 triangles and 2 squares. A triangle has 3 sides and a square has 4 sides. Draw the shapes. How many sides are there altogether?
pre.w: Drawing the shapes and counting the sides is a good start. This is a first win for everyone.

pre.q: A box has 9 shapes: triangles (3 sides) and squares (4 sides). There are 31 sides altogether. How many squares? Say how you started: draw it, list it or make a table.
pre.w: Any start is welcome: drawing 9 shapes, listing "1 square, 2 squares ..." or a table. A guess that is checked counts.

invest.title: Staircase
invest.first: Easy first step: draw 3 steps and show the 3 ways: 1+1+1, 1+2 and 2+1.
invest.text: Mei climbs a staircase. She can take 1 step or 2 steps at a time. For 3 steps there are 3 ways: 1+1+1, 1+2 and 2+1. (a) Find ALL the ways for 4 steps. (b) Find ALL the ways for 5 steps. (c) Fill in a table for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 steps. What pattern do you see? Can you guess the number of ways for 6 steps?
invest.model: Number of ways: 1 step: 1, 2 steps: 2, 3 steps: 3, 4 steps: 5, 5 steps: 8 (brute-forced; 6 steps: 13). 4 steps: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, 2+2. Pattern: each number is the sum of the two before it (3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13). Look for: a list in order (all 1s first, then swap in a 2), a table, and the pattern spotted from the table. Do not name Fibonacci numbers unless a child asks.

whatif.q: Go further: what if the coin puzzle is 70¢ with exactly 5 coins (using 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ coins)? Can it be done? How?
